title: Escalation: streaming disconnects behind proxy / load balancer
summary: Customer escalated intermittent Redwood streaming disconnects and occasional partial tool arguments when requests traverse corporate proxy + edge load balancer. Redwood reviewed symptoms, confirmed likely idle timeout / proxy buffering behavior on SSE, and recommended specific proxy/LB config (disable response buffering, increase idle timeouts, keep-alive, HTTP/2 considerations) plus client-side mitigations (longer read timeouts, heartbeats, retry strategy that does not attempt to resume mid-stream). Redwood committed to ship updated troubleshooting guidance and add a short “behind proxies/LB” section to streaming docs, with copy/paste config hints for common stacks (Nginx, Envoy, ALB).
topics: Observed disconnect pattern (20–40s, sometimes ~2min) on SSE streaming
Corporate proxy buffering and idle timeout behavior
AWS ALB / NLB / Cloudflare and Nginx settings that affect SSE
SDK client timeout defaults and suggested settings
Tool-call argument deltas and why partial args happen on disconnect
Mitigation plan: proxy config + app retry + observability
questions: Is Redwood able to resume a stream if the connection drops mid-generation?
What headers or keep-alive behavior does Redwood rely on for SSE?
How should we handle partial tool-call arguments if the stream ends early?
Do you recommend HTTP/2 for streaming through our edge stack?
action_items: Dev Patel - Send customer a short checklist for SSE behind proxies (Nginx/ALB/Envoy) including disable buffering and idle timeout guidance (due 2026-02-07)
Allison Grant - Share recommended client timeout settings for Python/TS/Go and confirm current SDK defaults for streaming read timeout (due 2026-02-07)
Owen Phillips - Pull gateway metrics for customer org/request_ids from the last 7 days and confirm predominant disconnect reason codes (due 2026-02-08)
Maya Rios (Northpeak) - Try turning off proxy response buffering + raise idle timeout to 300s in staging and report results (due 2026-02-10)
Liam Chen (Northpeak) - Capture a HAR / TCP reset timing and confirm whether disconnect is proxy-side FIN/RST vs client abort (due 2026-02-10)
Dev Patel - File docs update PR / ticket to add “Streaming behind proxies/load balancers” section and include partial tool-args handling note (due 2026-02-12)
next_steps: Customer to test proxy/LB configuration changes in staging and share results + timings.
Redwood to send written guidance + example configurations and update public troubleshooting docs.
Schedule 30-min follow-up after staging test to confirm stability and discuss any remaining tool-call parsing edge cases.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Escalation: streaming disconnects behind proxy / load balancer
Date: 2026-02-06
Time: 10:30 AM Pacific
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees:
- Dev Patel (Redwood Inference)
- Owen Phillips (Redwood Inference)
- Allison Grant (Redwood Inference)
- Maya Rios (Northpeak Benefits)
- Ethan Cole (Northpeak Benefits)
- Priya Nandakumar (Northpeak Benefits)
- Liam Chen (Northpeak Benefits)

---

Summary (auto-generated):
Customer reports streaming disconnects when using Redwood Hosted API via SSE through corporate proxy and AWS load balancer. Redwood recommends disabling proxy buffering, increasing idle timeouts, and adjusting client timeouts. Redwood will update troubleshooting docs and share a configuration checklist.

Topics (auto-generated):
1) Streaming behavior and disconnects
2) Proxy buffering and load balancer timeouts
3) SDK configuration + retries
4) Tool-call argument deltas on disconnect

Action items (auto-generated):
- Redwood: send proxy/LB config checklist
- Customer: test config changes in staging
- Redwood: update docs troubleshooting section

---

[00:00] Dev Patel: Okay, cool. Thanks everyone for jumping on kinda last minute. Um, I’m Dev, I’m in Customer Success but I pull in eng when we get these. Owen is on escalations, Allison is reliability/observability. Maya, Priya, Ethan, Liam—thanks.

[00:18] Priya Nandakumar: Yeah, thanks for making time. This has been hurting us in prod for about a week.

[00:24] Dev Patel: Understood. Why don’t we start with what you’re seeing, and then we can map it to where it might be disconnecting. Maya, you wanna drive?

[00:33] Maya Rios: Sure. We’re using your streaming responses, SSE. In our app, we proxy the request through our edge—corporate proxy, then AWS load balancer. We see disconnects like, mid-response. We’ll get tokens for some seconds and then it just stops. Sometimes the SDK throws “connection closed” and other times it just ends and we don’t get like a final message object.

[00:56] Ethan Cole: And in tool calling, we’ll see partial JSON for tool args. Like it starts a tool call and then the args string is incomplete and our parser fails.

[01:08] Dev Patel: Got it. Two symptoms: stream disconnect and partial tool-call args. Both can be the same root cause if the socket drops mid-stream.

[01:16] Allison Grant: Yeah. For SSE it’s pretty common—any proxy buffering or idle timeout can make it look like the server stopped when really something in the middle closed it.

[01:27] Liam Chen: The tricky part is, it’s intermittent. It’ll work, then fail, and it’s worse during peak hours.

[01:34] Owen Phillips: When you say peak, do you mean you have more concurrency, or the generations are longer?

[01:39] Liam Chen: Both. We do longer completions sometimes—like 800, 1200 tokens—and concurrency goes up.

[01:47] Owen Phillips: Okay. On longer ones, any middlebox that has a short idle timer will bite you.

[01:52] Dev Patel: Can you share your rough network path? Like client -> ??? -> Redwood.

[02:00] Maya Rios: Browser hits our API gateway, then we hit an internal service in EKS. That service calls Redwood. Outbound egress goes through our corporate proxy appliance. Then we have an AWS ALB in front of the service. And I think there’s also Cloudflare at the very edge but that’s just for browser to us, not us to you.

[02:20] Allison Grant: Wait, ALB is in front of the EKS service but the outbound to Redwood goes through the corporate proxy. The ALB isn’t directly between you and Redwood, it’s between your browser and your service?

[02:30] Maya Rios: Correct. Sorry. The outbound from our service to you is corporate proxy then internet. But the streaming response we relay to the browser goes back through ALB.

[02:41] Allison Grant: That’s helpful. So you actually have two streaming legs: Redwood -> your service, then your service -> browser. Either can break.

[02:49] Ethan Cole: Exactly. We’re doing a pass-through where possible, but we do some event handling for tool calls.

[02:56] Dev Patel: That lines up with what support saw in the ticket. You mentioned disconnect after like 20 to 40 seconds sometimes?

[03:03] Maya Rios: Yeah, often around 30 seconds. Sometimes around 2 minutes.

[03:08] Owen Phillips: 30 seconds smells like a proxy read timeout or an L7 idle timeout. 60 seconds is another common default. 120 too.

[03:16] Liam Chen: The corporate proxy default idle is 30s, I believe. But we thought because it’s constantly sending tokens, it’s not idle.

[03:25] Allison Grant: It depends what the proxy considers “activity”. If it’s buffering, it might not flush to the client frequently, so from the *next hop* perspective it’s idle.

[03:36] Maya Rios: That’s interesting. We have Nginx in the EKS service too, and I think it buffers unless you disable it.

[03:44] Owen Phillips: Yeah, Nginx will buffer by default. For SSE you usually want `proxy_buffering off;` and also `proxy_cache off;` and `chunked_transfer_encoding on;` and make sure it’s not compressing in a weird way.

[03:58] Ethan Cole: We use Envoy in some places and Nginx in others, so… okay.

[04:03] Dev Patel: We can send a checklist for common stacks. But first, can I ask what SDK you’re using for Redwood? TS? Python?

[04:10] Maya Rios: TypeScript on the backend.

[04:12] Dev Patel: Okay. And then you stream to browser via fetch event stream.

[04:17] Maya Rios: Yeah.

[04:18] Allison Grant: In Node, there’s also the default socket timeout behaviors. Depending on what HTTP client you use under the hood, it might close if no data is read for X. But again if you buffer it, Node thinks nothing is coming.

[04:31] Owen Phillips: Do you have logs with request IDs? Our gateway emits `x-redwood-request-id` in headers and also in the final response object. If you’re not getting final response, you might still have the header on the initial handshake.

[04:43] Liam Chen: We have some request IDs but it’s inconsistent because when it disconnects we don’t always log the header.

[04:51] Dev Patel: Got it. Action item: if you can log the request id from the initial response headers, that helps us correlate.

[04:58] Priya Nandakumar: We can do that.

[05:00] Dev Patel: Okay. Let’s talk about the tool-call partial args. Ethan, what are you doing when you see tool call deltas?

[05:08] Ethan Cole: We basically concatenate `arguments` chunks until we get something that parses as JSON. But when the stream drops we end up with something like `{"userId": "123",` and then it never completes. We sometimes still try to run the tool and it fails.

[05:24] Allison Grant: Yeah, please don’t run the tool unless you have a complete validated JSON object. In our canonical patterns we recommend: accumulate deltas, then only parse on a “tool_call complete” signal or at stream end when you have a final tool call payload.

[05:39] Owen Phillips: And if the stream ends unexpectedly, treat any in-progress tool call as incomplete and retry the *whole* request rather than trying to salvage the partial tool args.

[05:48] Maya Rios: That makes sense but then how do we avoid double-charging or like duplicate side effects?

[05:55] Dev Patel: Good question. The key is: don’t do side effects until you have validated tool args. If a stream drops mid-generation, you can retry the request. For side-effecting tools, you can also implement idempotency keys in your own tool layer. But Redwood itself, we don’t have “resume from event id” today for the streaming generation.

[06:14] Maya Rios: So no resume/cursor.

[06:16] Owen Phillips: Correct. It’s not like a Kafka offset. If you lose the connection, you rerun the request. We can advise how to do that safely.

[06:25] Liam Chen: We’re also seeing sometimes the browser disconnects but backend keeps streaming from Redwood and then we’re wasting tokens.

[06:33] Allison Grant: That’s another common issue. You want cancellation propagation: if browser aborts, your backend should abort the upstream request to Redwood. In Node, use AbortController and pass the signal through; in Go, context cancel; in Python, close the stream.

[06:49] Ethan Cole: We do have AbortController but I’m not sure it’s wired all the way.

[06:54] Dev Patel: We’ll send a snippet.

[07:00] Priya Nandakumar: Before we go too deep—can you confirm if you’ve seen issues on your side? Like did something change recently?

[07:08] Owen Phillips: We haven’t seen a general incident. But we did ship additional metrics around disconnect reasons recently. Let me check… I can pull last 7 days for your org if you give me a time window.

[07:21] Dev Patel: From the ticket, it started around Jan 29?

[07:25] Maya Rios: Yeah, roughly.

[07:28] Owen Phillips: Okay. I’ll pull metrics by request id and by customer org. We classify disconnect as client abort, upstream timeout, proxy close, that kind of thing—best effort.

[07:43] Allison Grant: Also, a change on your side—like a proxy firmware update—can look like “Redwood started failing.” Not saying that’s what happened, but it’s typical.

[07:54] Liam Chen: We did have a security team change a proxy policy around that time. Could be related.

[08:01] Dev Patel: That’s a strong signal.

[08:03] Dev Patel: Can we get a bit more detail on the corporate proxy? Is it like Zscaler, BlueCoat, something else?

[08:10] Liam Chen: It’s Zscaler for egress.

[08:12] Allison Grant: Zscaler is notorious for buffering and for timeouts on long-lived connections unless configured. SSE can look like “long response” and it tries to optimize.

[08:23] Maya Rios: Is there a header we can set to force it to not buffer?

[08:27] Allison Grant: Some proxies respect `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `X-Accel-Buffering: no` (that’s Nginx-specific). For Zscaler it’s more policy-based. But on your own Nginx/Envoy you can disable buffering and flush frequently to keep everything “active.”

[08:45] Owen Phillips: On the Redwood side, we send SSE events as they’re produced. But if your layer buffers, your downstream won’t see them.

[08:53] Ethan Cole: We might be doing gzip compression too.

[08:56] Allison Grant: Yeah, disable gzip for event-stream. Compression + buffering is basically guaranteed to batch data.

[09:03] Dev Patel: Okay, let’s do a concrete checklist for your service -> browser leg. Maya, what is fronting that? ALB and Nginx ingress?

[09:11] Maya Rios: ALB ingress controller, then service.

[09:14] Owen Phillips: ALB has an idle timeout default of 60 seconds. If the connection has no bytes transferred for 60 seconds, it will close. If your Nginx buffers and doesn’t flush, ALB sees nothing.

[09:29] Liam Chen: We can bump ALB idle timeout to 300 seconds.

[09:32] Dev Patel: Great. We usually recommend >= 300s for streaming.

[09:36] Allison Grant: And make sure your server writes something at least every, say, < 15 seconds. If tokens are slow, you can send an SSE comment line like `: keep-alive\n\n` just to keep the pipe active. Some frameworks support that.

[09:54] Ethan Cole: We can do that on the service -> browser leg.

[09:58] Maya Rios: But on the Redwood -> service leg, we can’t force tokens if the model is thinking.

[10:03] Owen Phillips: In practice the model emits tokens steadily, but yes tool call planning can have gaps. Also, if you request a huge response, there might be longer internal phases. It’s not common but it happens.

[10:16] Allison Grant: Another knob is: reduce max tokens and use iterative calls, but that’s product-level.

[10:21] Priya Nandakumar: We’d rather fix infra first.

[10:24] Dev Patel: Totally.

[10:26] Dev Patel: For Redwood -> service: what HTTP library are you using in TS?

[10:31] Maya Rios: We’re using your SDK, which uses fetch under the hood, I think.

[10:35] Allison Grant: Node fetch on older Node versions can have odd behavior with streaming unless you’re on Node 18+ / 20 and using undici. What Node version?

[10:46] Maya Rios: Node 18.19.

[10:49] Allison Grant: That’s okay. Still, make sure you’re not setting a global request timeout of 30 seconds somewhere.

[10:56] Liam Chen: We might have a default in our service mesh.

[11:01] Owen Phillips: If Envoy is in the path, check `stream_idle_timeout` and `idle_timeout`. SSE needs those raised or disabled for that route.

[11:11] Ethan Cole: We do have an Envoy sidecar. I’ll check.

[11:15] Dev Patel: Perfect.

[11:18] Dev Patel: Let’s talk about how you detect stream end. You said sometimes “final message missing”. Are you relying on a particular event?

[11:27] Maya Rios: We’re looking for a `done` event, and then we parse the final JSON. But sometimes it just ends without `done`.

[11:36] Owen Phillips: If the connection drops, you won’t get the done sentinel. So you should treat EOF without done as failure.

[11:44] Allison Grant: And in our updated examples we recommend capturing the final response object when it arrives, but if it doesn’t, you log that as incomplete and retry.

[11:56] Maya Rios: Okay. We currently treat EOF as success, which is probably wrong.

[12:00] Dev Patel: That would explain silent truncation.

[12:04] Priya Nandakumar: The reason we did that is because in some older snippet it said the stream closes naturally. Maybe we copied an older doc.

[12:12] Dev Patel: Yep. We’re actively updating those docs; part of why this escalation is useful. We’ll make the troubleshooting explicit: “EOF without done/final response = retry.”

[12:26] Maya Rios: Great.

[12:28] Dev Patel: Liam, can you share any LB/proxy logs? Like does it show 499/504 or connection reset?

[12:35] Liam Chen: We see 504 sometimes on the ALB when the browser is connected. And in our service logs we see “socket hang up”. For the egress proxy, it’s harder, but Zscaler logs show something like “policy timeout”.

[12:53] Owen Phillips: That’s consistent with idle timeout.

[12:56] Allison Grant: 504 from ALB means it didn’t get a response from the target in time, but in streaming it can also be “no bytes” for the idle window.

[13:07] Ethan Cole: So disable buffering and flush often.

[13:10] Allison Grant: Exactly.

[13:12] Dev Patel: Okay, quick pause. I’m going to summarize the likely fixes, and you tell me if this matches your setup.

[13:18] Dev Patel: 1) On ALB: increase idle timeout to 300s (or more).
2) On Nginx/Envoy: disable response buffering for SSE routes, disable gzip, ensure immediate flush.
3) On corporate proxy: ask security team to allow long-lived event-stream connections to api.redwood… domain, or set policy exception.
4) In your backend: propagate abort/cancel so you don’t keep paying when browser disconnects.
5) In tool calling: never execute tool with partial args; treat incomplete stream as failure.

[13:52] Maya Rios: Yes, that matches.

[13:54] Priya Nandakumar: Yep.

[13:56] Liam Chen: Makes sense.

[13:58] Dev Patel: Great.

[14:00] Owen Phillips: One more: if you have HTTP/2 anywhere, some proxies do weird things with SSE on H2. It usually works but… if you suspect that, try forcing HTTP/1.1 between certain hops.

[14:13] Maya Rios: Interesting. Our browser to ALB might be H2.

[14:17] Allison Grant: H2 is fine typically. The bigger issue is buffering. But if you see it only on one path, testing H1 can isolate.

[14:28] Ethan Cole: On the Node side, we can control it. On the browser side, not really.

[14:32] Dev Patel: For now, prioritize buffering/timeouts.

[14:36] Dev Patel: Can we talk about the partial tool args again? Are you using parallel tools?

[14:41] Ethan Cole: Sometimes. We do a “search” tool plus a “get_user_profile” tool, and the model can call both.

[14:49] Owen Phillips: If multiple tool calls are interleaved, you need to aggregate per tool_call_id. If you just concat everything, it’ll break.

[14:58] Ethan Cole: We do per id, yeah.

[15:00] Allison Grant: Great. Still, if the stream is cut, you might end on a partial JSON boundary. The safe pattern is: buffer strings, attempt parse only when you receive a tool-call “completed” indicator, or if you have a final response object that includes the full arguments.

[15:16] Maya Rios: Do you send a “tool_call completed” event?

[15:19] Owen Phillips: In the canonical event model, you’ll see deltas, then eventually you’ll get a final tool call payload in the completed response. In some SDKs we also expose an explicit event when the tool call is finalized. But, if you’re consuming raw SSE, you might not have a single “completed” event. You basically treat “done” as: you now have the final.

[15:40] Ethan Cole: Okay. So until done, don’t assume valid JSON.

[15:44] Dev Patel: Exactly.

[15:46] Priya Nandakumar: What about retries? If we retry the whole request, do we risk different output and confusing UX?

[15:54] Allison Grant: There is some nondeterminism unless you set a seed and keep parameters stable. But if it’s failing, the alternative is truncated output. For UX, you can show “reconnecting…” and retry once.

[16:08] Owen Phillips: Also, if you’re doing structured outputs, you can validate and retry only when invalid. But for general chat, a retry is the only option on disconnect.

[16:19] Maya Rios: We do have a “JSON schema mode” for one endpoint.

[16:22] Dev Patel: Different topic, but similar pattern: validate, retry with a short repair prompt. We’ll keep this call focused on streaming stability.

[16:33] Liam Chen: Can you share what timeouts your SDK uses? Like read timeout.

[16:38] Allison Grant: In TS, we don’t enforce a short read timeout for streaming by default, but your environment might. We’ll confirm exact defaults and send a recommended config: e.g., don’t set a 30s overall timeout for streaming, set connect timeout but let read be long, and use AbortController with an upper bound you choose.

[16:58] Dev Patel: We’ll send that in writing.

[17:01] Maya Rios: Another detail: our proxy sometimes buffers until it has like 4KB. So we’ll see nothing, then a bunch of tokens.

[17:09] Owen Phillips: That’s exactly buffering behavior.

[17:12] Allison Grant: For SSE, you want flush per event. Each event is small, sometimes a few dozen bytes. Buffering to 4KB defeats it.

[17:24] Dev Patel: Okay. Let’s capture the concrete configs.

[17:28] Dev Patel: Maya, do you have an Nginx config snippet?

[17:31] Maya Rios: Not handy, but I know we use ingress-nginx with annotations.

[17:37] Allison Grant: In ingress-nginx, there are annotations like `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"` and `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600"` and `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "3600"`. Not sure if those are exactly, but yes, we can provide a template.

[17:57] Liam Chen: We can set those per path.

[18:00] Owen Phillips: And for Envoy, set `stream_idle_timeout: 0s` (meaning disabled) or a high value, and set `idle_timeout` high as well.

[18:10] Ethan Cole: Okay.

[18:12] Dev Patel: For ALB idle timeout: easy.

[18:15] Priya Nandakumar: Our security team will ask: is SSE supported officially? Any guidance from you?

[18:22] Dev Patel: Yes, it’s supported. We’re actually updating our docs specifically because of these issues. We’ll add an explicit section “Streaming behind proxies/load balancers” with settings.

[18:35] Allison Grant: Also we can provide language like: “SSE requires end-to-end support for long-lived HTTP responses; intermediate proxies must not buffer and must allow idle timeouts long enough.”

[18:47] Priya Nandakumar: Perfect.

[18:49] Dev Patel: Great.

[18:51] Dev Patel: Owen, anything you want to ask to help diagnose from our side?

[18:55] Owen Phillips: Yes. Maya/Liam, do you see disconnects when you run the same request from a machine outside the corporate network? Like from a direct AWS box or local with no proxy.

[19:06] Maya Rios: When I run it from my home network with curl, it’s stable.

[19:10] Owen Phillips: That’s strong evidence it’s the proxy/edge path.

[19:14] Liam Chen: We also ran from a bastion that bypasses Zscaler and it was fine.

[19:19] Allison Grant: Great.

[19:20] Dev Patel: So the fix is squarely on the proxy/LB path and our docs.

[19:25] Ethan Cole: Can we do anything in the request headers to help? Like keep-alive?

[19:30] Allison Grant: Standard SSE headers: `Accept: text/event-stream` (the client sets), and server sends `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, `Cache-Control: no-cache`, `Connection: keep-alive`. We already set the server side ones. But your proxy might override.

[19:47] Owen Phillips: You can also ensure you don’t set `Accept-Encoding: gzip`.

[19:53] Maya Rios: Okay.

[19:55] Dev Patel: Let’s talk about timeline. Can you test the ALB + ingress changes in staging today or early next week?

[20:02] Maya Rios: We can do today in staging.

[20:05] Liam Chen: Yeah, we can bump timeouts and turn off buffering in staging quickly.

[20:10] Dev Patel: Great. If it stabilizes, we’ll mirror in prod with your normal change management.

[20:17] Priya Nandakumar: We’ll need a short writeup to attach to our change request.

[20:22] Dev Patel: We’ll send that. Action item on me.

[20:25] Allison Grant: Also, to validate: run a long streaming request, like 1500 tokens, and measure if it survives for, say, 10 minutes.

[20:34] Maya Rios: Okay.

[20:36] Ethan Cole: And tool calling?

[20:38] Allison Grant: Once the stream stops disconnecting, the partial tool args should mostly disappear. But still update your code to not treat EOF as success.

[20:49] Ethan Cole: Yep, we’ll patch that.

[20:52] Dev Patel: Great.

[20:54] Dev Patel: While we’re here, I want to address the “final message missing” comment. In streaming, there are two common patterns. One is: the stream includes all data and then you get a final object event. Another is: you only get deltas and you build the final yourself. Our current recommendation is: consume events, build state, and also handle the final response if present. But you should not assume the stream closing equals completion.

[21:21] Maya Rios: Understood.

[21:23] Owen Phillips: And if you’re building state, make sure you handle out-of-order tool deltas. Some proxies can merge lines; it’s rare but we’ve seen it.

[21:33] Ethan Cole: Hmm, okay.

[21:35] Allison Grant: That’s why we recommend an SSE parser that respects event boundaries and doesn’t do line-based hacks.

[21:42] Maya Rios: We’re using an eventsource library on the browser side.

[21:46] Allison Grant: That’s usually fine.

[21:48] Dev Patel: Okay.

[21:50] Dev Patel: I’m going to pause for a second—any other symptoms? Like specific error codes? 502? 499?

[21:57] Liam Chen: We see 499 sometimes, which I think is client closed.

[22:01] Owen Phillips: Right. 499 is Nginx client abort. That can happen if browser gives up.

[22:07] Allison Grant: Or if a proxy closes and Nginx thinks the client closed.

[22:11] Dev Patel: Okay.

[22:13] Priya Nandakumar: Also, the disconnects are more frequent on mobile networks.

[22:18] Allison Grant: Mobile networks are flaky. That’s where retry UX helps. But your issue seems more correlated with corporate path.

[22:27] Dev Patel: Yep.

[22:29] Dev Patel: Owen, do we have anything we can do server-side to keep it alive more aggressively? Like ping comments.

[22:35] Owen Phillips: Not today. The gateway emits events as generated. We’ve discussed adding periodic heartbeat comments, but it’s a behavior change. For now we document how to handle through proxies.

[22:48] Dev Patel: Okay.

[22:50] Allison Grant: But you can implement heartbeat on the second leg (your service -> browser) even if upstream is quiet, as long as you don’t mislead. It keeps ALB alive.

[23:01] Maya Rios: Good point.

[23:03] Ethan Cole: We can send comment pings.

[23:06] Dev Patel: Great.

[23:08] Dev Patel: Let’s set next steps. Today: you test disabling buffering + raising idle timeouts in staging. We send checklist and recommended settings. Owen pulls metrics from our side.

[23:21] Maya Rios: Works.

[23:23] Priya Nandakumar: Can we schedule a follow-up early next week?

[23:27] Dev Patel: Yes, I’ll send a calendar hold for Monday or Tuesday.

[23:31] Liam Chen: Monday afternoon is good.

[23:33] Dev Patel: Cool.

[23:35] (brief crosstalk)

[23:38] Allison Grant: One more thing—if your service is relaying streaming, ensure you’re not reading the entire upstream into memory. Some frameworks will buffer response bodies unless you use streaming APIs explicitly.

[23:50] Maya Rios: We do use streams, but I’ll double-check.

[23:53] Ethan Cole: We had a bug where we were awaiting the full text. We fixed that, but maybe in some branch it’s still there.

[24:01] Owen Phillips: If that happens, it would look like a big delay then sudden close.

[24:06] Dev Patel: Okay.

[24:08] Dev Patel: Any concerns from security/compliance about SSE?

[24:12] Priya Nandakumar: Mostly about proxies. They want to inspect traffic.

[24:16] Allison Grant: They can still inspect; it’s HTTPS. But if they MITM, it can break streaming. If they do SSL inspection, they might re-chunk traffic.

[24:29] Liam Chen: They do SSL inspection.

[24:31] Owen Phillips: That’s likely the culprit.

[24:34] Dev Patel: If they do TLS interception, you’ll want an explicit exception for the Redwood endpoint for streaming, or at least configure it to not buffer.

[24:45] Priya Nandakumar: Okay, we’ll take that back.

[24:48] Dev Patel: Great.

[24:50] Dev Patel: I think we’re aligned. Owen, anything else from your side?

[24:54] Owen Phillips: Just: please send us a couple request ids from failures if you can. Even if it’s just the handshake header.

[25:01] Maya Rios: We will.

[25:03] Dev Patel: Allison, you’ll send client guidance.

[25:06] Allison Grant: Yep.

[25:08] Dev Patel: Okay, then we’ll wrap.

[25:11] Priya Nandakumar: Thanks all.

[25:13] Dev Patel: Thanks everyone.

---
